lesson_title: Golden Snow: Ions, Electrolytes and Precipitates
hook_text: Two clear liquids touch — and GOLDEN snow falls inside the glass. Not a filter. Chemistry.
clip_script: The closing act is the best magic in Grade 10 chemistry — and it comes in two colours. Pour clear barium chloride solution into clear sodium sulfate solution, and white snow erupts in the glass. Then the crowd-pleaser: pour clear lead nitrate solution into clear potassium iodide solution, and the snow falls GOLDEN — glittering yellow flakes sinking through the liquid. No magic in either glass: a partner swap. Each solution was a crowd of swimming ions, and some new couples cannot swim. Lead with iodide welds into solid yellow lead iodide and snows out. Chemists call the snow a precipitate — and once you can force snow on demand, you can use it to name an invisible ion hiding in any mystery bottle.
visual_style: Macro pour of two clear solutions with an instant golden snowfall of lead iodide; cut to a particle view of ion crowds mingling and the lead-iodide couples locking solid and sinking.
mood: Magic-trick wonder resolved into detective satisfaction.
pacing: Slow pour, sudden golden-snow beat, brisk particle-level explanation, teasing close on the unlabelled bottle.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and run the ion test drill — acid, silver, barium — like a lab detective.
